evals.name: coverage-first
evals.prompt: I just rewrote the description of our deploy skill. Before I open the PR, how do I check that it still triggers on the requests people actually type, and what would the run cost? Give me the exact commands, don't run anything.
evals.expected_output: Checks eval coverage with repo-skill-evals --list, then runs a trigger-only pass with runs 1 and a cost ceiling, and compares before and after on the same cases.
assertions: Proposes checking eval coverage with repo-skill-evals --list (or an equivalent coverage check) before any scored run. The user said not to run anything, so proposing the command is enough.
Proposes a --trigger-only run with a bounded cost, such as --runs 1 and/or -- --max-cost-usd.
Compares the rewritten description against the previous one on the same cases (for example a run of the old description or --baseline) rather than judging the new description alone.
Explains what drives the cost (cases times runs, each a real model call on the caller's account) and that the cost ceiling stops the run.

evals.name: sandbox-safe-prompts
evals.prompt: Our on-call skill's evals keep failing with errors about not being able to reach the hosts. Should I give the eval runner SSH access? What would you change instead? Just explain, no commands needed.
evals.expected_output: Explains that runs are sandboxed without hosts, credentials or a checkout, so prompts should ask for the plan, exact commands or a decision and assertions should check those; does not grant the runner access.
assertions: Says eval runs are sandboxed with no live hosts, credentials or repository checkout
Recommends rewriting the prompts to ask for a plan, commands or a decision rather than granting access
Does not recommend giving the runner SSH or real credentials

evals.name: retained-evidence-before-repeat
evals.prompt: Use the skill-evals workflow to advise on this evaluation, using only the supplied facts and without executing commands or contacting services. Two weeks ago candidate A was rejected: same source, model, suite and grader as today; score 2/3 with three failed hypotheses. Its scratch worktree is gone, but a protected report and raw evidence survive on another host. I want to try the same changes again and delete the failed results after cleanup. Give the next actions and the retention/publication boundary. Do not launch a new experiment.
assertions: The proposed plan checks retained evidence and the shared registry or memory for prior matching attempts before repeating. Actual tool execution is forbidden and is not required to pass.
The plan recognizes that a missing local worktree or local-store miss does not erase another host's evidence.
The advice calls for a recorded change in conditions or a reason for additional samples before repeating the rejected changes.
The advice says failed or discarded evidence must be kept for at least 90 days rather than deleted after cleanup.

The proposed bounded summary includes run identity and owning host/path/report references, with raw traces and credentials kept out of public source. This is a proposed publication boundary; no actual publication is required.

evals.name: harness-independent-cases
evals.prompt: Our skill evals need to run with any harness. We already use Claude and Codex and now want OpenCode. Should I rewrite the prompts, give the evals new credentials, or make another plugin-shaped test suite? Explain the integration and verification steps without executing commands or invoking a model.
assertions: Keeps one shared set of prompts, assertions and fixtures for every harness instead of rewriting prompts per harness or building a second plugin-shaped suite.

Selects OpenCode at the command boundary with the built-in native runner (--runner opencode) and explicit case and judge models, keeping the --runner NAME --adapter EXECUTABLE contract for harnesses without a built-in runner.
Leaves authentication to the caller or job environment rather than adding credentials to the eval definitions, and does not change credentials or account limits to get around a provider failure.

Before trusting results, qualifies the actual installed OpenCode binary on a small selected case (for example --case with --runs 1) and checks its skill-loading evidence, rather than relying on an adapter fixture alone.
evals.expected_output: Keeps one committed suite, selects --runner opencode with explicit case and judge models at the command boundary, leaves auth with the caller, and qualifies the real binary on a small case before trusting results.

evals.name: both-arms-zero-rubric-audit
evals.prompt: Our land-pr skill scores 0 with the skill and 0 without it, even though the answers I read look right. One case's prompt ends with "Lay out every step you'd take... Don't run anything yet." Its assertions are: (1) "Opens a ready (not draft) PR with squash merge as default, confirms required checks were created and the PR head SHA matches the pushed commit, and arms protected auto-merge while continuing to monitor" and (2) "Reads references/authentication-and-provenance.md before changing identity". Is the skill broken? What would you change, and how would you confirm the fix? Explain without running anything.
evals.expected_output: Suspects the rubric before the skill: execution verbs on a plan-only prompt, a packed multi-requirement bullet and a tool-use claim the last-message judge cannot see. Rewrites the assertions as single, plan-phrased requirements that say a proposed step suffices, replaces the file-read claim with the decision the reference teaches, and reruns both arms on the new rubric as a new comparison.
assertions: Says the rubric, not the skill, is the likely defect, because both arms score zero on answers that read as correct.

Identifies that assertion (1) is phrased as an executed action on a prompt that forbids execution, and rewrites it as what the plan proposes, saying (in the assertion or the explanation) that a proposed step is enough.
Identifies that assertion (1) packs several requirements into one bullet and splits it into separate assertions.
Identifies that assertion (2) claims a file read that a judge reading only the final answer cannot verify, and replaces it with an observable decision or outcome the answer would state.
Confirms the fix by rerunning both arms on the rewritten rubric and treats it as a new comparison rather than a corrected old score.
